_superseded_reasoning_2026_09_07._decision: EXTEND THE GUARD AS A RATCHET; DO NOT SCRUB HISTORY. Recorded 2026-09-07 for GitHub #146, which asked for a decision either way rather than continued silence.
_superseded_reasoning_2026_09_07._note_on_the_last_line: 'The population may shrink freely' is what made this scrub compatible with the ratchet mechanism itself -- only the DECISION needed reversing, not the guard.
_why_ratchet_and_not_a_scrub: MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED: the host name is load-bearing NOWHERE. All 55 occurrences across 37 tracked files are prose -- docstrings, workflow comments, audit narrative -- plus exactly one self-test fixture value in check_runner_label_coverage.py. Runners are selected by LABELS (self-hosted, Windows, X64, pdfe-windows, pdfe-builder) in `runs-on:`, never by host name. The issue listed six files as 'plausibly load-bearing'; reading them shows none is.

So a scrub is technically possible. It is still the wrong trade: ~25 of the files are historical audit and disposition documents, and rewriting narrative evidence to remove a machine label damages the record for a small gain. This repo keeps those documents precisely because they say what was true on the day.

A host name is also not a personal identifier. The account name is a person (and their email local-part); two history rewrites were proportionate for that. The bare name identifies a machine, and the repo already publishes far more specific operational detail about that machine in tools/runner-deployment/.

The real risk is GROWTH, and specifically MACHINE-GENERATED growth. ConformanceChecker::flushConformanceRecord() has already written host identity into a tracked docs/ file on every suite run, taking occurrences from 0 to 9 AFTER a history rewrite. During phase 9 of this same pipeline a committed pytest artifact added another (a JUnit `hostname` attribute pytest emits automatically). Neither was noticed by a human. A ratchet catches exactly that class.
So: existing occurrences are accepted and named here; new ones fail. The population may shrink freely.

_what: Zero-tolerance ratchet for the self-hosted runner's HOST NAME in tracked files (GitHub #146). check_tracked_path_hygiene.py enforces that the build ACCOUNT name never appears anywhere; this file is the host-name counterpart. As of 2026-10-19 the accepted population is EMPTY: the host name has been scrubbed from every tracked file except the three that must name it to police it, so any occurrence is now a failure.
_why_a_length_is_stored: PERFORMANCE, and it costs nothing real. Hashing every token of every tracked file cost 66 s per run (9.9M tokens over 3,596 files) and timed out the fast-checks pytest batch at exit 124. `n` is the character length of the hashed string, so the matcher skips any token or pair of a different length without hashing it -- which eliminates well over 90% of the calls. It does not weaken anything meaningfully: a sha256 of a short lower-case token is brute-forceable in seconds whether or not its length is written down, so hashing here buys protection from CASUAL READING of a tracked file, not protection from a determined search. That is the same property scrub_needles.json has always had, stated plainly rather than implied.
_why_hashed: Converted 2026-10-24. The plaintext host name is gone from this file. A guard that names what it forbids reintroduces it -- the same reason scrub_needles.json has always been hashed. Verify a needle with: sha256 of the LOWER-CASED token, or of two adjacent tokens joined by a single space, UTF-8. This is the scrub guard's tokenising rule, reused so the two halves of this checker cannot disagree.
_why_the_2026_09_07_decision_was_reverse: The 2026-09-07 reasoning was sound ON ITS OWN TERMS and is kept in full under `_superseded_reasoning_2026_09_07`. It weighed a machine label against the damage of rewriting ~25 historical audit documents, and concluded the label was not worth it.

WHAT CHANGED IS THE CONTEXT, NOT THE REASONING. That decision was taken for a PRIVATE repository, where the host name is visible only to people who already have the machine. pub-readiness is preparing this repository to be made PUBLIC (GitHub #200), which converts 'a machine label in an audit document' into permanent public operational detail about a named build host.

The pipeline's phase-5 criterion asked for 0 hits, which directly contradicted this file. Rather than let a register row silently override an issue-tracked decision -- the repository's own rule is that the issue wins -- the conflict was put to the owner with both sides and the measured population. The owner chose to scrub.

The 2026-09-07 claim that the name is load-bearing NOWHERE was re-verified before scrubbing, not taken on trust: every occurrence in tools/ops/*.ps1, the workflows and the gate scripts is a comment, docstring or self-test fixture value. Runners are still selected by LABELS in `runs-on:`, never by host name. One self-test fixture value in check_runner_label_coverage.py was updated with the rest and the suite stayed green.
_why_the_names_are_listed_here_rather_th: DCA 0047. The account check takes its needle from USERNAME/USER/LOGNAME at run time; on the GitHub ubuntu runner that is `USER=runner`, which matched 365 tracked files in a repo full of runner tooling, went red for five commits, and hid four real failures underneath. Deriving a host-name needle from COMPUTERNAME would repeat that exactly -- the CI host is not this host. The names are therefore an explicit, reviewable list.
_why_this_file_still_names_the_host: IT NO LONGER DOES. Superseded 2026-10-24: the needle is hashed, so the baseline, the checker and the checker's tests all stop naming the host and HOSTNAME_SELF_EXEMPT is removed. The previous text read 'a ratchet needs its needle', which was true of a PLAINTEXT needle only.
